standard.title: Use comprehension strategies
standard.description: use comprehension strategies such as visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising and questioning to understand and discuss texts listened to, viewed or read independently
standard.prior_knowledge: Students listen to and view texts in classroom read-alouds. They have not yet been explicitly taught comprehension strategies as named, deliberate moves that can be applied intentionally to construct meaning.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can use a range of comprehension strategies — visualising, predicting, connecting, summarising, questioning — when listening, viewing and reading, and can discuss texts using what they have understood.

nodes.label: Predicting uses what we know
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can make a prediction about what a text will be about using available information (title, cover, images).
nodes.minimum_width: Make one prediction about a text before reading, using the title or cover image.
nodes.typical_width: Predict what might happen in a text based on title and cover; connect predictions to prior knowledge; revisit predictions after reading.
wider: Make predictions at multiple points in a text — before, during, and after — comparing how predictions change
Make predictions about texts from unfamiliar cultural contexts and discuss what prior knowledge was and wasn't useful
success_criteria: Student makes a prediction with reasoning — using a visible text feature (title, image) to justify the prediction.
Student can revisit and evaluate their prediction after reading.

nodes.label: Connecting links text to experience
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can make a connection between a text and their own experiences or prior knowledge.
nodes.minimum_width: Make one connection between a text and their own life or prior knowledge.
nodes.typical_width: Connect texts to personal experiences; identify similarities and differences between text events and own life; use connections to deepen understanding.
wider: Make text-to-text connections — identifying how two texts are similar or different
Connect texts to knowledge from other learning areas — identifying when prior curriculum knowledge helps understand a text
Make connections to First Nations Australian stories and cultural accounts when engaging with relevant texts
success_criteria: Student makes a connection between a text event and their own experience.
Student can explain how the connection helped them understand the text.

nodes.label: Retelling and summarising shows understanding
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can retell or summarise key content from a text they have listened to, viewed or read — selecting what was most important.
nodes.minimum_width: Retell at least two key events or facts from a text in sequence.
nodes.typical_width: Retell stories using picture cues or prompts; relate one or two key facts from informative texts; sequence events in retelling; retell events from First Nations Australians' stories in sequence.
wider: Retell the same text in two different modes (oral and drawing) and compare what each captures
Summarise an informative text by identifying and reporting the most important facts — distinguishing from interesting details
Retell events from First Nations Australian cultural accounts attending to cultural sequence and significance

response_modes.reason: Retelling accurately and sequentially is a fundamental comprehension output skill — precision matters and sequence errors signal comprehension gaps. Practice across multiple text types builds accuracy.

success_criteria: Student retells at least two key events or facts from a text in the correct sequence.
Student's retelling captures the main content, not just an interesting detail.

nodes.label: Questioning deepens understanding
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can ask a genuine question about a text — identifying something they want to understand or find out more about.
nodes.minimum_width: Ask one question about a text listened to or read (e.g. 'Why did the character do that?').
nodes.typical_width: Ask questions about texts before, during and after reading; listen for specific purposes — to answer a given question or find a specific detail; generate and pursue genuine questions.
wider: Generate questions about a text and discuss which questions the text answers and which it doesn't — exploring how texts have limits
Listen to a text for a specific purpose set by the teacher and then for a purpose generated by the student — comparing the experience
Ask questions about texts from culturally unfamiliar contexts — identifying what additional knowledge is needed to fully understand them

response_modes.reason: Questioning as a comprehension strategy risks becoming rote ('ask a question') rather than genuinely purposeful. Multiple text types — including informative and First Nations Australian texts — help students develop questioning as a real meaning-making move.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Developing genuine questioning — distinguishing literal from inferential questions, pursuing questions the text does not answer — offers rich metacognitive development for advancing students beyond the Foundation-level expectation.
success_criteria: Student asks at least one genuine question about a text — not just a yes/no question.
Student can identify whether their question was answered by the text or requires another source.
Student can listen to a text with a specific question in mind and report the answer.
